name: The Antikythera Mechanism
context: c. 100 BCE — recovered from a Greek shipwreck in 1901. The oldest known analog computer: 37 meshing bronze gears that predict planetary positions, lunar phases, and eclipses decades in advance.

name: Leonardo's 1490 To-Do List
context: In one of his notebooks, Leonardo listed tasks: 'Get the master of arithmetic to show you how to square a triangle. Ask Giannino the Bombardier about the tower of Ferrara. Find a master of hydraulics and get him to tell you how to repair a lock, canal, and mill in the Lombard manner.' A mind in perpetual apprenticeship.

name: The Jacquard Loom Punch Card
context: Invented 1804 by Joseph-Marie Jacquard. Punched cards told the loom which threads to lift — binary logic encoded in paper a century before computers. Babbage was inspired by it. So was Hollerith's census machine.

name: Feynman's Problem-Solving Notebook
context: Feynman kept notebooks as an extension of thinking, not a record of it. When told his notebooks were his work, he replied: 'No, the work is in my head. The notebooks are the work.' The distinction matters.

name: The Rosetta Stone
context: Carved 196 BCE, found 1799. The same royal decree in three scripts — hieroglyphic, Demotic, Greek. Its genius was redundancy: the same message in three languages became the key to 1,400 years of lost writing. Translation as a gift across time.

name: Babbage's Difference Engine Fragment
context: Designed 1819, never finished in Babbage's lifetime. The Science Museum built it in 1991 from his original drawings — it worked perfectly. Some ideas are simply ahead of their manufacturing base.

name: Shannon's 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' (1948)
context: 77 pages in the Bell System Technical Journal. Shannon invented the bit, defined entropy, set the theoretical limits of compression and transmission. In the acknowledgments, he thanked no one — he had invented an entire field alone.

name: Pacioli's Double-Entry Ledger (1494)
context: Luca Pacioli codified double-entry bookkeeping in Summa de arithmetica — invented by Venetian merchants. Every transaction recorded twice, from two perspectives. It made the invisible visible: the same idea that drives modern observability.

name: The Index Card
context: Invented by Carl Linnaeus in the 1760s to reorganize his taxonomy notes — the same flexible unit that became the backbone of Luhmann's Zettelkasten, the library card catalog, and the recipe box. One atom of thought, movable and linkable.

name: View from the Window at Le Gras (c. 1826)
context: The oldest surviving photograph, taken by Joseph Nicéphore Niépce using an 8-hour exposure on pewter. The smearing of light across the rooftops captures an entire day compressed into a single moment.

name: Alan Turing's Bombe Machine (1940)
context: Designed to crack German Enigma-encoded messages. At Bletchley's peak, 211 Bombes decoded over 3,000 messages per day. Turing never published a paper on it — the entire project was classified for decades.

name: Dewey's First Classification Scheme (1876)
context: Melvil Dewey published his system as a 42-page pamphlet. The insight: any knowledge domain can be given a decimal address, allowing infinite subdivision without reorganizing the whole. Still used in 95% of US public libraries.

name: The Lascaux Cave Paintings
context: Created approximately 17,000 years ago in the Dordogne. Over 600 animals rendered with anatomical precision — foreshortening, motion blur — by people with no written language. Visual intelligence at full resolution.

name: The First Telegraph Message (1844)
context: 'What hath God wrought' — sent by Samuel Morse from Washington to Baltimore on May 24, 1844. The first words sent faster than a horse could carry them. Distance suddenly became a variable, not a constant.

name: Newton's Prism Experiment (1666)
context: Newton proved that white light contains all colors — the prism doesn't add color, it reveals it. The prevailing view had it backwards. He bought the prism at a fair, curious about the colors he saw in it.

name: The Eames Lounge Chair Design Process (1956)
context: Charles and Ray Eames spent a decade on the lounge chair — hundreds of material experiments, plywood studies, prototype failures. The final form looks inevitable. It took ten years to look that way.

name: Bamboo Strip Tao Te Ching (300 BCE)
context: The oldest known Tao Te Ching was found on bamboo strips in a 300 BCE tomb. Scholars discovered that in this version, 'Virtue' (Te) comes before 'Way' (Tao) — inverting the canonical chapter order and suggesting a different interpretive tradition.

name: The Voynich Manuscript
context: A 15th-century illustrated codex written in an unknown script. Despite analysis by cryptographers, linguists, and AI systems, it has never been decoded. It may be a constructed language, a cipher, or an elaborate hoax. The mystery is itself the artifact.

name: The Voyager Golden Record Cover Diagram
context: The pulsar map etched onto both Voyager spacecraft encodes our location in the galaxy using 14 pulsars as reference points, plus a hydrogen spin-flip as the unit of time. A whole civilization's return address in line art — designed to be self-decoding.

name: The First UNIX man Page (1971)
context: Written by Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson. 'man ls' — the original manual page established the convention of machine-readable, human-readable documentation co-located with the software. Every `man` command since is a direct descendant.
